guides.title: Fix Wi-Fi & Network Disconnections on Linux (NetworkManager & nmcli)
guides.symptom: Linux Wi-Fi shows 'No Wi-Fi Adapter Found', network drops constantly, or DNS fails
guides.description: Diagnose wireless adapter states, manage NetworkManager via `nmcli`, restart networking daemons, and install missing proprietary Wi-Fi firmware.
causes: Missing proprietary Broadcom, Realtek, or Intel wireless firmware drivers
guides.whyItWorks: Most modern Linux systems manage connections using NetworkManager. Restarting the daemon re-polls PCI/USB buses. Checking `rfkill` unblocks software radio locks, and installing `linux-firmware` supplies the binary blobs needed by modern Wi-Fi chipsets.

steps.instruction: Check for software/hardware radio blocks with `rfkill`
steps.detail:
Run this command in terminal:
rfkill list
If Wi-Fi shows 'Soft blocked: yes', unblock it with:
sudo rfkill unblock all
Then verify with `rfkill list` that all blocks are removed.

Restart the network daemon to reinitialize adapter interfaces:
sudo systemctl restart NetworkManager
Wait 5 seconds and check connection status with:
nmcli device status

Check your physical hardware chipset to verify if the kernel recognizes it:
lspci -knn | grep -iA 3 net
Or for USB dongles:
lsusb
Look at the 'Kernel driver in use' and 'Kernel modules' lines. If no driver is shown, you need to install proprietary drivers.

steps.instruction: Install missing proprietary firmware (Broadcom / Realtek / Intel)
steps.detail:
On Ubuntu/Debian, connect temporarily via Ethernet or phone USB tethering and run:
sudo apt update && sudo apt install --reinstall linux-firmware
For Broadcom Wi-Fi cards (very common on laptops):
sudo apt install bcmwl-kernel-source -y
Reboot your system after installation.

guides.title: Diagnosing Failed Services with Systemd & Journalctl
guides.symptom: A background service (web server, docker, database, SSH) fails to start or crashes
guides.description: Troubleshoot service failures on modern Linux systems using `systemctl status`, systemd unit dependencies, and `journalctl` error logs.
causes: Port conflict with another running daemon (e.g. port 80 or 443 already bound)
Configuration syntax error in unit file or app configuration (e.g. nginx.conf)
File permission mismatch on service data directories
guides.whyItWorks: `systemd` is the init system that supervises background services in Linux. When a service fails, systemd retains the exit code and crash logs in the binary journal (`journalctl`), pinpointing the exact configuration line or socket collision that caused the crash.

steps.instruction: Inspect failed systemd units across the system
steps.detail:
List all currently failing services:
systemctl --failed
Note the exact unit name (e.g., `apache2.service` or `docker.service`).

steps.instruction: Check the detailed status and last exit code
steps.detail:
Run status on the specific service:
systemctl status target_service.service
Check the 'Active:' state (e.g. failed/activating), Main PID, and the last 10 log entries printed directly below the status output.

Examine the full recent error traceback for the failed unit:
journalctl -xeu target_service.service
Press Shift+G to jump to the very bottom (most recent messages). Look for lines with 'Failed to bind', 'Permission denied', or 'syntax error'.

steps.instruction: Restart or reload the service after configuration fixes
steps.detail:
Once configuration issues are resolved, reload systemd daemon files and restart the service:
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart target_service.service
Verify with `systemctl is-active target_service` (should output 'active').

guides.title: Finding & Killing High CPU & Memory Runaway Processes (htop & kill)
guides.symptom: Linux system is sluggish, CPU fan is spinning loud, or system becomes unresponsive
guides.description: Identify process resource hogs using `htop` and `ps`, resolve zombie/hung processes, and monitor swap usage.
causes: Memory leak in an application triggering high swap thrashing
Infinite loop thread consuming 100% of a CPU core
guides.whyItWorks: Linux uses POSIX signals for process lifecycle control. Sending `SIGTERM` (15) allows clean state cleanup, while `SIGKILL` (9) forcefully terminates runaway threads directly at the kernel scheduler level.

steps.detail:
Install and launch `htop`:
sudo apt install htop -y && htop
Press F6 to sort by CPU% or MEM%. The top bars show per-core utilization and RAM/Swap usage in real time.

steps.instruction: Find process by command line with `ps`
steps.detail:
If you know the app name (e.g., chrome or python), find its Process ID (PID):
pgrep -l app_name
Or get top 5 memory hogs:
ps aux --sort=-%mem | head -n 6

First attempt a graceful termination (SIGTERM):
kill PID_NUMBER
If the process remains unresponsive after 5 seconds, force terminate it (SIGKILL):
kill -9 PID_NUMBER
steps.warning: `kill -9` immediately ends execution without saving open work. Only use it when normal quit attempts fail.
